Lesson 5 · Business route

Uncertainty and conditional comparisons

Do powered fixtures improve calibration output across service ages?

The business problem

A calibration manager wants to know whether powered fixtures are worth buying for more rigs. Existing fixture rigs have higher output, but they are also older on average. The capital decision is about future purchases for a particular mix of rigs, not about explaining one headline gap. The manager needs an estimate of extra output that can be paired with equipment price, installation downtime, maintenance, and remaining service life.

What the data show

The unadjusted fixture comparison is 10.45 units per hour. After a simple service-age adjustment it is 2.49. The change shows why the comparison group matters.

The raw fixture gap and the age-adjusted gap answer different questions because they compare different rig mixes. Looking at rigs of similar age brings the result closer to the investment decision. The fuller analysis lets the fixture difference vary with service age, so finance can calculate payback for the ages it actually operates. A gain that pays for itself on a heavily used rig may not repay the cost on a rig nearing retirement.

What would you decide?

Compare rigs of similar age and bench setting, and allow the fixture difference to vary with age. Report an effect for a specified rig rather than one universal number.

Identify rig ages and operating conditions where the expected extra output could cover the purchase. Pilot fixtures on a small set of suitable rigs under a recorded assignment rule. Measure hourly output, downtime, maintenance, and technician time over the same follow-up period. The investment memo can then show expected payback by rig type and explain which assets should be considered first.

Pause and explain

What should the investment memo show instead of one average fixture coefficient?

Compare your reasoning

Show expected output gain and payback for rigs of relevant ages, along with installation, maintenance, and remaining-life costs.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

In the generator, the fixture difference is 5 units per hour at six years of service and changes by 1.1 units for each additional year. One fitted coefficient need not equal that whole effect function.

The bigger picture

An average return is rarely the whole capital case. The right purchase can depend on asset age, utilization, installation cost, and time left to recover the investment. Showing the gain for a specified rig turns a regression result into a portfolio decision: where should limited funds go first? This way of thinking also applies to training, maintenance, and technology upgrades. The next lesson shifts from estimating an equipment relationship to building a procedure that can support many future decisions at the moment they arise.
